title: Build a reusable data-fetching hook
scenario: You're on the platform team for a coaching marketplace (think find-a-coach, book-a-session). Every screen — coach profile, learner dashboard, admin review queue — hand-rolls its own `useEffect` + `useState` fetch logic, and it's grown inconsistent: some screens forget loading states, others double-fetch on every render. Your lead asks you to extract a single `useFetch` hook that the whole app can standardize on before the next sprint touches the admin dashboard.
requirements: Accept a URL (or null to skip fetching) and return { data, error, isLoading }
Re-fetch automatically when the URL changes, and support a manual refetch() function
Avoid setting state after the component has unmounted
Support an options object (headers, method) without re-fetching on every render due to a new object reference
Type the hook generically so callers get typed data: useFetch<Coach[]>(url)
Do not leak the previous URL's response when the URL changes quickly
bugs:
- The effect depends on `options`, but callers pass a fresh object literal on every render (`{ headers: ... }`), so the effect re-runs and refetches on every keystroke/render — an infinite fetch loop in practice.
- There is no cleanup: if the component unmounts (or the URL changes) before the fetch resolves, it still calls setState, causing "Can't perform a React state update on an unmounted component" warnings and, worse, race conditions where a slower earlier request overwrites a later one's data.
- There's no way to manually refetch (e.g. after a mutation) and no support for skipping the fetch when `url` is null (e.g. waiting on an id from a route param).
- No generics/typing, so every consumer has to cast `data` themselves.
explanation: The core fix is decoupling "what triggers a refetch" from "what configures the request." The effect's dependency array now only lists `url` and an internal `reloadToken`, both stable primitives, so a new inline options object per render no longer causes an infinite refetch loop; the options are read from a ref at call time instead. A local `cancelled` flag closed over by the effect's cleanup function guards every `setState` call, so a stale response from a superseded request (or one that resolves after unmount) is silently dropped instead of corrupting state. `refetch` is exposed by bumping a counter that's part of the dependency array, which is a clean way to force a re-run without duplicating the fetch logic. Passing `null` as the URL is treated as "don't fetch yet," which matches the common pattern of waiting for a dynamic route param or an auth token before fetching. Generics let every call site get typed data without a manual cast at the call site.
tradeoffs: This hand-rolled hook is fine for one or two data shapes per screen, but it re-implements caching, deduping, and background refetching that a library like TanStack Query or SWR already solves robustly (stale-while-revalidate, window-refocus refetch, query key based caching across components). The AbortController approach (aborting the actual fetch on cleanup) is more correct than a boolean flag because it also cancels the network request itself, not just the state update — worth mentioning as a follow-up improvement. Storing options in a ref sidesteps the re-render loop but means the hook won't automatically refetch if a header value (like an auth token) changes; a real fix is to depend on the specific primitive values that matter (e.g. `token`) rather than the whole options object.
followUps: How would you add request deduplication if two components call useFetch with the same URL simultaneously?
Why is an AbortController better than a boolean "cancelled" flag here, and how would you wire it in?
How would this hook interact with React 18 Strict Mode double-invoking effects in development?
How would you extend this to support polling every N seconds?

title: Prevent stale API responses (race conditions on fast param changes)
scenario: On an agriculture marketplace, a buyer searches for "wheat" listings and rapidly changes filters — region, then crop type, then price range — while typing. The listings grid flickers and occasionally shows results for a filter combination the user already changed away from, because a slow earlier request resolves after a faster later one. Support has filed this as "search results don't match my filters" and it's now a P1 for the team.
requirements: Ensure only the response matching the latest filter state is ever rendered
Cancel (or ignore) in-flight requests when filters change before they resolve
Avoid a flash of stale data followed by a flash of loading state on every keystroke
Keep the fix scoped to the fetching logic, not a full rewrite of the filter UI
Work correctly under React 18 Strict Mode (effects mounting twice in dev)
bugs:
- No cancellation or "is this still current" check — every fetch that resolves calls setState, including ones for filter values the user has since changed away from. If request A (wheat, region=X) is slow and request B (wheat, region=Y) is fast, B's results render first and then get overwritten by A's stale results.
- `filters` is likely a new object reference every render from the parent (e.g. built inline in JSX), which can cause the effect to fire more often than intended — worth confirming filters is memoized or primitive-keyed upstream.
- No AbortController, so slow requests keep consuming bandwidth/server resources even though their result will never be used.
- No error handling at all.
explanation: The fix has two parts. First, an `AbortController` is created per effect run and its `signal` is passed to `fetch`; the cleanup function aborts it whenever the effect re-runs (filters changed) or the component unmounts, so a stale in-flight request is actually cancelled at the network layer rather than merely ignored. Second, the `AbortError` is caught and swallowed silently, since it represents "this request was intentionally superseded," not a real failure — showing an error for it would be wrong. Depending on the individual primitive filter fields (`filters.crop`, `filters.region`, etc.) instead of the whole `filters` object also avoids re-running the effect due to a new object reference with the same values, which is a common source of extra fetches when filters are constructed inline by a parent. Rendering the grid "dimmed" during reloads instead of unmounting it avoids the loading-flash/content-flash flicker UX bug on every keystroke.
tradeoffs: AbortController cancels the network request cleanly but does add a small amount of boilerplate per fetch site; a data-fetching library (TanStack Query, SWR) handles this by keying requests on the filter values and automatically cancelling/deduping superseded queries, which is usually the better long-term answer for a whole app. Debouncing the filter changes upstream (e.g. 300ms after the user stops typing) reduces the number of requests fired in the first place and is complementary to, not a replacement for, cancellation — you still need cancellation for slow network conditions. An alternative to AbortController is a monotonically increasing "request id" ref compared on resolution, which works without server/browser abort support but doesn't actually cancel the underlying network call.
followUps: Why is checking err.name === "AbortError" necessary — what happens without it?
How would debouncing the filter input interact with this cancellation logic?
How does TanStack Query solve this problem internally, and what would migrating this component to it look like?
What would you check first if this same "stale data" bug were reported for a search-as-you-type autocomplete instead of a filter panel?

title: Build protected routes (Next.js App Router)
scenario: You're building the audit firm's internal dashboard where auditors review client filings before submission. Anyone who isn't logged in should never see the `/dashboard` section, even for a flash of a frame, and should be redirected to `/login` with a way to return to where they were headed. A contractor's first pass works "most of the time" but QA found that refreshing directly on `/dashboard/clients/42` briefly shows dashboard content before redirecting.
requirements: Redirect unauthenticated users away from any route under /dashboard before content renders
Preserve the originally requested URL so the user lands back there after login
Work correctly on both client-side navigation and a hard refresh/direct URL load
Avoid a flash-of-protected-content on the initial server render
Explicitly note that this client/edge-level check is a UX convenience, not a security boundary — the API must independently verify auth on every request
bugs:
- This is a client component that checks auth in a `useEffect`, which only runs after the initial render/hydration — so on a direct load or refresh of a protected URL, the (empty) dashboard shell and any child content can briefly render/hydrate before the redirect kicks in, exactly what QA saw.
- Auth state lives only in `localStorage`, which isn't available during SSR, forcing this client-only, post-hydration check in the first place.
- The redirect to `/login` doesn't preserve the originally requested path, so after logging in the user lands on a generic dashboard home instead of `/dashboard/clients/42`.
- There's no server-side enforcement mentioned at all here — if this is the *only* check, a user could hit the underlying API routes directly and get data regardless of the UI redirect.
explanation: Moving the check into Next.js `middleware` means it runs at the edge, before any React tree (server or client) is rendered — so there is no flash-of-protected-content because the protected page's HTML is never produced or sent for an unauthenticated request; the browser gets a redirect response instead. Using an `httpOnly` cookie instead of `localStorage` for the session token is what makes this possible, since middleware runs outside the browser and can read cookies on the incoming request but has no access to `localStorage`. The original path is captured as a `redirectTo` query param on the way to `/login` and consumed after a successful login to send the user back to where they intended to go. Critically, this is still only a routing/UX guard: every API route and server action the dashboard calls (e.g. fetching client 42's filing data) must independently verify the session cookie and the caller's authorization on the server, because middleware can be bypassed by anyone calling the underlying endpoints directly — the middleware protects the page shell, not the data.
tradeoffs: Middleware is the right layer for coarse "logged in or not" gating since it runs once at the edge for every matched request, but it's a poor place for fine-grained, per-resource authorization (e.g. "can this auditor see this specific client") because it usually can't cheaply check that without an extra data round trip; that check belongs in the page's server component or the API route itself. An alternative is per-page server-component checks (`const session = await getSession(); if (!session) redirect('/login')`), which is more flexible for resource-level checks but must be repeated on every protected page/layout, risking one being missed. Cookie-based sessions require CSRF consideration for state-changing requests, whereas a header-based bearer token (common with client-heavy SPAs) avoids CSRF but forces the localStorage/no-SSR-check trade-off this lab exists to fix.
followUps: Where would you put the check for "this auditor can view this specific client's filing" versus "this user is logged in at all"?
How would you handle an expired-but-present session cookie differently from a missing one?
What changes if you need role-based access (auditor vs. reviewer vs. admin) on top of this?
Why can middleware read cookies but not localStorage, and how does that shape where session tokens should live?

title: Implement role-based UI rendering (RBAC)
scenario: The coaching marketplace has three roles — coach, learner, and admin — sharing large parts of the UI (session details page, messaging, payouts). Product wants coaches to see a "Cancel session" and "Reschedule" button, learners to see "Join call" and "Leave review," and admins to see everything plus a "Force refund" action, all on the same underlying `SessionDetailPage` route.
requirements: Centralize role-check logic instead of scattering role === "..." conditionals through JSX
Support checking a single role or "any of" a set of roles for a given UI element
Make it easy to add a new role (e.g. "support-agent") without touching every component
Hide admin-only actions from the DOM entirely for non-admins, not just visually disable them
State explicitly that this client-side rendering logic is a UX layer only — the backend must independently enforce authorization on every mutating endpoint
bugs:
- Role logic (which buttons a role can see) is duplicated inline per role branch, so adding a fourth role or changing "who can reschedule" means editing this component (and every other one that repeats the same pattern) in multiple places — easy to get inconsistent across the app.
- There's no single source of truth mapping permissions to roles, so a security review or a support ticket like "why can support-agent not issue refunds" requires grepping JSX across the codebase.
- No mention/enforcement anywhere that the server independently checks permissions — if this is the only gate, a learner could call the cancelSession or forceRefund API directly.
- No handling for a user with no matching role (falls through silently, which is fine, but not intentional/documented).
explanation: The fix replaces per-component `role === '...'` branches with a single permissions map (`ROLE_PERMISSIONS`) that's the one place encoding "who can do what." Components ask "can this user perform X?" via `can()`/`usePermission`, never "is this user role Y?", which decouples UI code from the specific set of roles — adding `support-agent` or changing what admins can do is now a one-line change in the map, not a hunt through JSX. The `<Can>` component returns `null` rather than a disabled/hidden element when the check fails, so unauthorized actions never enter the DOM (no risk of a curious user un-hiding a button via devtools and calling the handler — though see the trade-off below on why that alone still isn't a security boundary). The route handler example is the actual enforcement point: it re-runs the same `can()` check against the authenticated user resolved server-side from the session/token, independent of anything the client sent, which is what actually prevents a learner from issuing a refund by hitting the API directly.
tradeoffs: A static role→permission map like this is simple and fast but doesn't handle resource-level rules well (e.g. "a coach can cancel only their own sessions, not any session") — that needs an additional ownership check, typically done server-side against the resource being acted on, not just the role. For more complex policies (time-based permissions, org hierarchies, delegated admin), a policy engine (CASL, OPA) or attribute-based access control might be worth the added complexity; for three to five roles and a fixed action set, the map above is usually the right amount of abstraction. Hiding disallowed UI is good UX (no dead buttons users can click and get an error), but the only thing that actually prevents unauthorized actions is server-side enforcement — this is worth saying out loud in an interview even though it feels obvious, because it's the detail juniors most often skip.
followUps: How would you extend this to resource-level checks like "only the assigned coach can cancel this specific session"?
Where exactly should the permissions map live if both the Next.js frontend and a separate backend service need to agree on it?
What happens if a user's role changes (e.g. demoted) while they have an active session with a stale JWT — how do you handle that?
How would you test that Can correctly hides content for each role without duplicating the permissions map in your tests?

title: Build a multi-step React Hook Form + Zod validation flow
scenario: The agriculture marketplace's "List your farm for an event" flow was originally a single giant form and converts poorly — farmers abandon it. Product wants it split into three steps (Farm details, Produce & pricing, Review & submit) with per-step validation, the ability to go back without losing data, and a final submit that only fires once all steps pass.
requirements: Define one Zod schema per step plus a combined schema for final submit
Persist form values across step navigation (back/forward) without resetting fields
Block advancing to the next step until the current step's fields are valid
Show field-level error messages as the user types/blurs, not only on submit
Disable the submit button while the request is in flight and show a clear failure state on server error
bugs:
- No validation at all — a user can click "Next" with empty fields and reach step 3, and the only server feedback comes after a failed submit at the very end, defeating the point of splitting into steps.
- Each step manages its own local useState fields disconnected from a shared form; nothing stops step 2's fields from being blank if the user navigates back and the component remounts and loses local state (React Hook Form + a shared context/wizard-level form instance would persist this correctly).
- No pending/error state around the final submit — the button stays clickable during the request (risk of duplicate submissions) and there's no feedback if the POST fails.
- Steps don't share one form instance, so cross-step reads (e.g. showing farm name on the review step) rely entirely on manually threaded formData props, and per-field errors aren't shown inline as users type.
explanation: A single `useForm` instance is created at the wizard level and shared via `FormProvider`/`useFormContext`, so field values persist naturally across steps — going back to step 1 shows exactly what was typed because there's one form state, not three disconnected `useState` calls that get thrown away on remount. Per-step validation is achieved by calling `trigger(fieldsForThisStep)` on "Next," which validates only the named fields against the merged Zod resolver and blocks navigation until they pass, while the final submit uses `handleSubmit`, which runs the full schema and only calls `onSubmit` if everything (across all steps) is valid — protecting against a user who somehow reaches step 3 with stale data. `formState.isSubmitting` is used to disable the submit button and show a spinner during the request, and a local `submitError` state renders a clear failure message with the button re-enabled on error so the user can retry without losing anything they entered. Field-level errors render inline from `formState.errors`, updating on blur (`mode: 'onBlur'`) rather than only on final submit.
tradeoffs: Splitting one Zod schema per step plus a merged full schema adds a little duplication versus one flat schema, but it's what makes "next" validate only the current step instead of the whole form, which matters a lot for UX in long wizards. An alternative to `react-hook-form`'s `trigger()` per-step approach is a state machine (XState) per step with its own local form, syncing to a parent reducer on each transition — more explicit but heavier for a 3-step form. Persisting wizard progress to `sessionStorage` (so a refresh doesn't lose data) is a common follow-up ask; it's not included here to keep the core validation logic clear, but is worth mentioning as a natural next iteration.
followUps: How would you persist wizard progress across a page refresh without adding a backend draft-save endpoint?
How does zodResolver merge per-step errors with the full schema when only some fields are visible at a time?
What would you change if step 2's valid options depended on step 1's answers (e.g. crop list depends on region)?
How would you unit test that "Next" is blocked when step 1 is invalid, without spinning up a browser?

title: Implement optimistic updates with rollback
scenario: On the coaching marketplace's learner dashboard, marking a session as "attended" (which unlocks a review prompt) currently waits for the server round-trip before updating the checkbox, and on a slow connection it feels broken — users tap it twice, creating duplicate requests. Product wants the checkbox to flip instantly and silently revert (with a toast) if the server rejects it.
requirements: Update the UI immediately on user action, before the server responds
Roll back to the previous state and show an error toast if the request fails
Prevent duplicate submissions if the user taps again while a request is in flight
Keep the optimistic update local to the affected item, not a full list refetch
Reconcile with the server's actual response once it arrives (in case the server value differs from the optimistic guess)
bugs:
- No rollback: if the PATCH request fails, `attended` stays flipped in the UI forever even though the server never persisted it, silently desyncing client and server state.
- `!attended` is read twice (once for setAttended, once for the request body) from a stale closure — if handleToggle somehow fires twice quickly the second call reads the same pre-toggle `attended` value, sending the wrong intended state.
- No in-flight guard: rapid double-clicks fire two overlapping PATCH requests with no ordering guarantee about which one "wins" on the server, and no disabling of the checkbox while a request is pending.
- No error surface to the user (no toast/notification) so a silent failure looks like success.
- Doesn't reconcile against what the server actually returns (server might apply business rules, e.g. can't mark attended before the session start time).
explanation: The handler captures `previous` (the pre-toggle value) and `next` (the intended value) once, up front, so both the optimistic UI update and the request body use consistent values instead of re-deriving `!attended` from a potentially stale closure. The checkbox flips immediately via `setAttended(next)` for instant feedback, and `isPending` both disables the input and short-circuits `handleToggle` if it fires again mid-request, eliminating duplicate submissions from a double-tap. On failure, the catch block resets state to `previous`, restoring exactly what the user saw before their action, and a toast makes the failure visible instead of silent. On success, the code re-reads the server's actual returned value (`serverState.attended`) and applies it rather than trusting the optimistic guess forever — this matters because the server may apply rules the client doesn't know about (e.g. rejecting "attended" before the session's scheduled start time), so the final UI state should always be the server's truth, with the optimistic value only bridging the gap until it arrives.
tradeoffs: This per-row local state approach is simple and fine for a single toggle, but if attendance also needs to update aggregate counts elsewhere (e.g. a "sessions attended" stat on a parent dashboard), the optimism needs to happen at whatever state layer those aggregates are derived from (context, a query cache) rather than purely locally — otherwise the aggregate won't update until the parent refetches. A library like TanStack Query's `useMutation` with `onMutate`/`onError`/`onSettled` formalizes exactly this optimistic-update-plus-rollback pattern and handles query cache invalidation/reconciliation for you, which is usually preferable once more than one place in the app needs to reflect the same mutation. Disabling the checkbox during the request is the simplest guard against duplicate submits; a more advanced alternative is request de-duplication/debouncing at the network layer, useful if the same action can be triggered from multiple UI entry points simultaneously.
followUps: How would you adapt this if toggling "attended" also needs to update a session count shown elsewhere on the same page?
What would you change if the PATCH could be slow (seconds) rather than typically fast — should the UI behave differently?
How does TanStack Query's useMutation onMutate/onError/onSettled map onto the rollback logic you wrote by hand here?
How would you test the rollback path without actually hitting a flaky network?

title: Design reusable loading/error/empty state components
scenario: Across the ERP system's dozens of list and detail screens (purchase orders, vendors, inventory adjustments), every team has implemented its own version of "show a spinner, then either an error, an empty state, or the content." The patterns are all slightly different, making the app feel inconsistent, and a recent audit found three different spinner components in the codebase. You're asked to design one shared pattern the rest of the app can adopt incrementally.
requirements: Provide a single component (or hook pattern) that renders loading, error, empty, or content states from one shared status
Make the empty state distinct from the error state (e.g. "no purchase orders yet" vs "failed to load")
Allow each screen to customize copy/actions per state without duplicating the state-switching logic
Support a retry action wired to the error state
Keep it composable with any data source (REST hook, WebSocket, local state) rather than coupled to one fetch implementation
bugs:
- The loading/error branching logic is copy-pasted per screen with slightly different markup each time (three spinners, inconsistent error messages), which is the exact problem being fixed.
- There's no empty state at all: an empty `data` array silently renders an empty list, which users read as a broken page rather than "you have no purchase orders yet."
- No retry action on error — the user's only recourse is a full page refresh.
- The component is tightly coupled to `useFetch`'s specific return shape, making it hard to reuse for a WebSocket-driven or locally-computed data source that has its own way of expressing loading/error/data.
explanation: The design centers on a single discriminated union, `AsyncState<T>`, with exactly four statuses (`loading`, `error`, `empty`, `success`), and one component, `AsyncBoundary`, that switches on it — this is the one place the loading/error/empty branching logic lives, so every screen stops re-implementing it. Crucially, `AsyncBoundary` doesn't know or care where `state` came from: a small adapter function (`toAsyncState`) maps any data source's own shape (a REST hook's `{data, error, isLoading}`, a WebSocket hook's connection state, or a locally computed value) into the shared union, so the component is composable with anything. Per-screen customization (the "no purchase orders yet" copy and a "Create one" call-to-action) is passed in as props/fallbacks rather than being hardcoded, so screens get consistent structure with distinct content. The render-prop `children` function only receives `data` in the `success` case, which means TypeScript can narrow the type correctly — inside `children`, `data` is never `null`, eliminating a whole class of "data is possibly null" bugs at every call site. `onRetry` is threaded straight to the default error fallback (or a custom one), wiring "click retry" back to the original `refetch`.
tradeoffs: A single generic `AsyncBoundary` is a good default for most list/detail screens, but very custom screens (e.g. a dashboard combining three independent data sources with different loading timings) may need a different composition, like independently rendering each source's own `AsyncBoundary` rather than trying to force one combined status. Treating "empty" as its own state (versus folding it into "success" and letting each screen check `data.length === 0` itself) adds one extra case to design around, but pays for itself immediately once more than two screens need distinct empty-state copy — it stops "empty" from being forgotten, which was the original bug in VendorsList. This pattern intentionally doesn't try to solve caching, background refetching, or pagination — those are separate concerns that compose on top of (not inside) this state-rendering primitive.
followUps: How would you extend AsyncBoundary to represent a "stale-but-showing-cached-data-while-refetching" state, common with SWR-style libraries?
How would you unit test AsyncBoundary's four branches without wiring up a real data source each time?
What changes if two independent async sources feed one screen and you want a single combined loading spinner?
Why does making children a render-prop (data) => ReactNode help TypeScript here, versus just passing data as a prop?

title: Build a paginated API-backed table with request cancellation
scenario: The tax workflow dashboard has a "Filings" table with hundreds of thousands of rows across all clients. It supports page navigation, a status filter, and a client-name search. QA found that switching pages quickly, or typing a search term fast, sometimes shows a page of results that doesn't match the currently selected filter — a race condition similar to lab 2 but compounded by pagination state.
requirements: Fetch the correct page of results whenever page, pageSize, filter, or search changes
Cancel in-flight requests that are superseded by a newer filter/page/search change
Reset to page 1 when the filter or search term changes (but not when only the page changes)
Show a loading indicator without unmounting the existing table (avoid layout shift/flicker)
Debounce the search input so every keystroke doesn't fire a request
bugs:
- No request cancellation: rapidly changing filters/search/pages fires overlapping requests, and whichever resolves last wins regardless of whether it corresponds to the current UI state — the exact race condition QA reported.
- Every keystroke in the search box fires a new request immediately (no debounce), multiplying the race-condition surface and hammering the API.
- Changing the status filter or search term doesn't reset `page` back to 1, so a user filtering to "overdue" while on page 5 of "all" gets an out-of-range or mismatched page instead of seeing page 1 of the new filtered set.
- The table unmounts nothing today, which is fine, but there's no "dimmed while reloading" treatment — combined with the race condition, users see the old page's rows, then a flicker, then possibly the wrong new rows.
explanation: Search input is split into an immediate `searchInput` (bound to the text field so typing feels instant) and a debounced `search` value used only for fetching, via a small `useDebouncedValue` hook that delays committing the value by 300ms of inactivity — this collapses a burst of keystrokes into a single request. A separate effect watches `status` and the debounced `search` (deliberately excluding `page`) and resets `page` to 1 whenever either changes, which correctly distinguishes "the filter changed, start over" from "the user is just paging through the current filter." The main data-fetching effect uses an `AbortController`, cancelling any in-flight request in its cleanup whenever `page`, `status`, or `search` changes again before the previous request resolved — this is what actually eliminates the race condition, since a superseded request's `AbortError` is caught and ignored rather than allowed to overwrite `rows`/`total`. The table is dimmed (not unmounted) during reloads and pagination controls are disabled while loading, avoiding layout shift and preventing a user from queuing up multiple rapid page changes.
tradeoffs: Debouncing the search value delays the request slightly (300ms), which is the right trade for reducing load and race-condition surface on a search-as-you-type field, but would be wrong for something like a submit button where immediacy matters more than request volume. Keeping pagination "page 1 on filter change" logic in a separate effect (rather than folding it into the fetch effect) makes the two concerns easier to reason about independently, at the cost of one extra render before the fetch effect re-runs with the corrected page — negligible in practice. For a table this central to the product, migrating to TanStack Query/TanStack Table with a paginated query key (`['filings', page, status, search]`) would get cancellation, caching (instant back/forward paging), and retry for free, at the cost of adopting a new dependency across the ERP dashboard.
followUps: Why must the "reset to page 1" effect exclude page from its own dependency array, and what would happen if it didn't?
How would you cache already-fetched pages so navigating back to page 1 doesn't re-fetch it?
How would you keep the URL in sync with page/status/search so refresh and back-button preserve state (ties to lab 19)?
What's the risk of debouncing the fetch itself (instead of the search value) in this design?

title: Build a WebSocket connection-status dashboard
scenario: The audit dashboard streams live filing-status updates over a WebSocket so auditors see changes (e.g. "client uploaded a document") without refreshing. Right now there's no visible indication of connection health, so when the socket silently disconnects (VPN hiccup, server restart), auditors keep working against a dashboard that's quietly stopped updating, and don't notice until they miss something time-sensitive.
requirements: Expose a clear connection status: connecting, connected, reconnecting, disconnected
Reflect status changes in the UI within one render (a banner or indicator dot)
Distinguish "reconnecting" (temporary, expected) from "disconnected" (gave up, needs user action)
Clean up the socket and any timers on component unmount to avoid leaks
Avoid setting React state from socket event handlers after unmount
bugs:
- There's no reconnection logic at all: once the socket closes for any reason (network blip, server restart, idle timeout), status goes straight to "disconnected" and stays there forever, with nothing attempting to reconnect — exactly the silent-failure scenario auditors reported.
- "disconnected" is used for both a transient close and a real give-up state, so the UI can't distinguish "reconnecting automatically, hang tight" from "connection lost, please refresh" — an important UX distinction called out in the requirements.
- `socket.close()` in cleanup is correct, but there's no guard against setting state after the effect has been cleaned up if a reconnect timer (once added) fires after unmount — worth flagging even though this starter has no timers yet, since it's the first bug someone adding reconnection would introduce.
- No exposure of a manual "retry now" affordance for the true disconnected state.
explanation: The status enum now has four distinct values, and `onclose` decides between `reconnecting` (attempt again, under `maxRetries`) and `disconnected` (give up) based on a retry counter, rather than collapsing every close into one terminal state — this directly fixes the UX ambiguity auditors experienced. Reconnection uses exponential backoff (`1000 * 2^retryCount`, capped at 30s) via `setTimeout`, and every handler checks an `isUnmounted` flag before calling `setStatus`, so a reconnect attempt that resolves after the component has unmounted never touches React state. The effect's cleanup clears the pending reconnect timer and closes the current socket, which prevents both a state-update-after-unmount warning and a leaked open socket/timer continuing to run in the background. The banner distinguishes the two failure modes visually and in copy — `reconnecting` is a low-key warning implying "hang tight," while `disconnected` is a hard error with an explicit recovery action, matching the requirement that a true give-up state needs user action.
tradeoffs: Exponential backoff capped at a max delay is a reasonable default, but for a dashboard where staleness has real time-sensitive cost (auditors missing a document upload), a shorter cap or a "resume aggressively for the first minute, then back off" curve might be worth the extra complexity — this is a product/reliability trade-off, not just a code one. Closing the socket manually inside `onerror` to funnel everything through one `onclose` retry path is simpler than duplicating retry logic in two handlers, at the small cost of one extra event round-trip. This lab intentionally keeps reconnection logic inline in the status hook; lab 10 factors it out with a cleaner "manual retry" API and message-queueing-during-reconnect, which is the natural next step for a production implementation.
followUps: Why is a ref (not state) the right place to store the retry count, and what would go wrong using state there?
How would you surface to the user roughly how many retries remain, or when the next attempt will fire?
What changes if multiple components on the page each need the connection status — would you lift this hook or share one socket via context?
How would you test the reconnect/backoff logic without waiting 30 real seconds in a test suite?

title: Implement WebSocket retry and reconnection logic with backoff
scenario: Building on the audit dashboard's live updates, the team wants a shared, well-tested `useWebSocket` hook other real-time features (ERP inventory alerts, coaching session chat) can reuse, rather than every feature re-implementing its own ad-hoc reconnect loop. It needs a real "retry now" action, message queueing while reconnecting, and to stop retrying forever if the network is simply gone (e.g. laptop closed for hours).
requirements: Reconnect automatically with exponential backoff and a maximum delay cap
Expose an explicit retryNow() the UI can call, resetting backoff state
Cap total retry attempts (or elapsed time) and surface a terminal "disconnected" state instead of retrying forever
Queue outgoing messages sent while disconnected/reconnecting and flush them once reconnected (or clearly document that this hook does not, if descoped)
Clean up all timers and the socket on unmount, with no state updates after unmount
bugs:
- The reconnect timeout creates a brand-new WebSocket but never attaches `onopen`/`onclose`/`onmessage` handlers to it, so after the first disconnect, the hook silently stops reacting to anything the "reconnected" socket does — status stays stuck on "reconnecting" forever even if the new connection succeeds.
- Fixed 1-second retry delay forever (no backoff, no cap) — a genuinely down server gets hammered with a reconnect attempt every second indefinitely, and there's no terminal "give up" state.
- `send()` silently drops messages if the socket isn't open (`socketRef.current?.send` just no-ops or throws depending on readyState) — no queueing, so a chat message typed while reconnecting is lost with no feedback.
- No `retryNow()` exposed, and the cleanup function calls `socket.close()` on the original socket variable, not `socketRef.current`, so if a reconnect has already replaced the ref, cleanup closes the wrong (stale) socket and leaks the new one.
explanation: `connect` is factored into a single reusable function (via `useCallback`) that both the initial effect and every subsequent reconnect attempt call, so the "reconnected" socket always gets its `onopen`/`onclose`/`onerror` handlers wired up identically — fixing the original bug where retries produced an inert socket. Backoff is capped by both `maxDelayMs` (30s) and `maxRetries` (8 attempts by default); once the cap is hit, `onclose` sets the terminal `disconnected` status instead of scheduling another retry, giving the UI a clear "stop and ask the user" signal. `retryNow()` resets the retry counter to zero and calls `connect()` directly, giving the UI an explicit, immediate recovery path independent of the backoff timer. Outgoing messages call `send`, which checks `readyState` and pushes to a `queueRef` array when the socket isn't open, and `onopen` flushes that queue in order the moment the connection is re-established, so a message typed mid-reconnect is delivered rather than silently dropped. `isUnmountedRef` is checked at the top of every handler, and cleanup clears the pending timer and closes `socketRef.current` (the *current* socket, not a stale closed-over variable), fixing the leak in the original cleanup.
tradeoffs: Queueing messages client-side is good for short reconnect gaps but risky for a long "disconnected" terminal state — queued messages could go stale (e.g. an outdated chat message sent minutes later) or accumulate unbounded memory if the user keeps typing while offline; a production version would cap queue size and/or expire queued messages after a timeout. Resetting `retryCountRef` to 0 on `retryNow()` means a manual retry always gets the fastest possible reconnect attempt, which is right for user-initiated recovery but means a flaky connection with a user mashing "retry" can still hammer the server — worth rate-limiting the button itself. This hook handles one socket per URL; a multi-feature app (ERP alerts + chat both open) sharing one physical connection would need a pub/sub layer on top so multiple consumers subscribe to one `useWebSocket` instance instead of opening N connections — a natural extension worth mentioning in an interview.
followUps: How would you rate-limit or debounce a user mashing the "Retry now" button?
How would you share a single underlying socket across multiple components/features instead of one per useWebSocket call?
What would you change about the message queue to avoid unbounded growth or stale message delivery?
How would you write a test for the exponential backoff timing without a real 30-second wait?

title: Build an Error Boundary wrapping a route/section
scenario: A rendering bug in one widget on the ERP's inventory dashboard (a chart component that throws when given malformed data from a legacy warehouse integration) currently crashes the entire page to a blank white screen, taking down unrelated widgets like the reorder-alerts panel that were rendering fine. The team wants that one widget to fail gracefully without affecting the rest of the dashboard.
requirements: Catch render-time errors thrown by a subtree and show a fallback UI instead of a blank screen
Scope the boundary narrowly (per-widget) so one failing widget doesn't take down the whole dashboard
Log the error (and component stack) to an error-reporting service
Provide a way to reset the boundary (e.g. "Try again" button) without a full page reload
Explain why this must be a class component (or use a library) since hooks cannot implement getDerivedStateFromError/componentDidCatch
bugs:
- There is no error boundary anywhere, so any render-time exception in any one widget propagates up through React and unmounts the entire tree beneath the nearest existing boundary (in this app, apparently none), producing a blank page for unrelated widgets too.
- Even if a boundary existed, error boundaries must be class components (React does not yet provide a hook equivalent of `getDerivedStateFromError`/`componentDidCatch`), so a naive attempt to "add a try/catch in the function component" would not work — render errors thrown by React's reconciliation aren't caught by JS try/catch around JSX.
- No error logging/reporting, so a production crash like this would only be discovered via user complaints, not monitoring.
- No recovery path — even wrapping in a boundary without a reset mechanism would leave the widget permanently broken until a full page reload.
explanation: `ErrorBoundary` is necessarily a class component because React's error-catching contract — `static getDerivedStateFromError` (to compute fallback state during the render phase) and `componentDidCatch` (to run side effects like logging after the error is caught) — is only exposed as class lifecycle methods; there is no hook equivalent as of the current React API, so this is one of the few remaining legitimate uses of a class component in a modern React codebase. Wrapping each widget individually (`<ErrorBoundary><StockLevelsChartWidget /></ErrorBoundary>`) rather than one boundary around the whole dashboard means a thrown error unmounts only that widget's subtree — `ReorderAlertsWidget` and `SupplierPerformanceWidget` keep rendering normally, which directly fixes the "one bad widget takes down the page" bug. `componentDidCatch` receives both the error and React's `componentStack` (which shows the component hierarchy at the point of the crash, distinct from a JS stack trace), and forwards both to `onError`, which the app wires to its actual error-reporting service. The `reset` method clears the caught error from state, causing `render` to attempt `children` again, which gives users a "Try again" affordance without a full page reload — useful when the underlying data was transient (e.g. a flaky API response) rather than a code bug.
tradeoffs: Error boundaries only catch errors thrown during rendering, in lifecycle methods, and in constructors of the tree below them — they do not catch errors in event handlers, async code (a rejected promise in a `useEffect`), or server-side rendering, so this pattern must be paired with try/catch in async code and cannot be the only error-handling strategy in the app. Per-widget boundaries (this lab's approach) give the most resilient UX but mean writing more boundary instances than one boundary per page; a middle ground is one boundary per "independent section" (e.g. per dashboard column) rather than truly per component, trading a little more blast radius for less wrapping boilerplate. Libraries like `react-error-boundary` provide this exact class implementation plus conveniences (a `resetKeys` prop that auto-resets when specified props change, e.g. when the underlying widget's data prop changes) — worth using in a real codebase instead of hand-rolling, though understanding the hand-rolled version (as here) is usually what's actually being tested in an interview.
followUps: Why don't error boundaries catch errors thrown inside a useEffect or an async event handler, and how would you handle those instead?
How would you automatically reset a widget's boundary when its underlying data prop changes, without a manual "Try again" click?
What's the difference between the JS error.stack and the componentStack you get in componentDidCatch, and why log both?
Where would you put boundaries in a Next.js App Router app that also has route-level error.tsx files?

title: Diagnose and fix unnecessary re-renders
scenario: The coaching marketplace's session chat panel has grown sluggish — typing in the message input causes the entire session sidebar (participant list, session timer, notes panel) to visibly re-render on every keystroke, based on React DevTools' profiler flame graph the team just captured. You're asked to find the cause and fix it without restructuring the whole component tree.
requirements: Identify why unrelated sibling components re-render when only the message input changes
Fix it using the appropriate combination of React.memo, useMemo, useCallback, or state colocation
Avoid over-memoizing everything defensively — explain which fixes are load-bearing versus unnecessary
Preserve existing behavior and props contracts (no breaking changes to child components)
Verify the fix conceptually against how React DevTools Profiler would show it (fewer highlighted re-renders)
bugs:
- `message` state lives in `SessionRoom`, the common ancestor of both `SessionSidebar` and `ChatPanel` — every keystroke triggers a re-render of `SessionRoom`, and even though `SessionSidebar` is wrapped in `React.memo`, it still re-renders because its props are not referentially stable across renders.
- `sidebarConfig` is a new object literal created on every `SessionRoom` render, so `config` is a new reference every time even though its contents never change — `React.memo`'s shallow prop comparison sees a "different" object and re-renders.
- `onKick={(id) => ...}` is a new inline arrow function every render, so the `onKick` prop also fails the shallow-equality check on every keystroke, defeating `React.memo` a second, independent way.
- The state that actually changes on keystroke (`message`) has nothing to do with the sidebar at all — this is a state colocation problem as much as a memoization problem: `message` should live as close as possible to where it's used (inside `ChatPanel` or an input-owning subcomponent), not in the shared parent.
explanation: The biggest win is state colocation: moving `message` out of `SessionRoom` and into `ChatPanel` means keystrokes only re-render `ChatPanel` itself — `SessionRoom` (the shared ancestor) no longer re-renders at all on typing, so `SessionSidebar` isn't even asked to reconcile, regardless of memoization. This is the load-bearing fix and, on its own, would already solve the reported problem, because `React.memo` and `useCallback`/`useMemo` only matter for a component that *is* re-rendering due to its parent; if the parent doesn't re-render, the child doesn't either. The remaining `useMemo`/`useCallback` around `sidebarConfig` and `handleKick` are still worth keeping as defense-in-depth: if `SessionRoom` ever re-renders for an unrelated reason (e.g. `participants` updates via a WebSocket event), those stable references ensure `SessionSidebar`'s `React.memo` shallow comparison actually succeeds and skips re-rendering it, rather than being defeated by fresh object/function references every time. The fix order matters conceptually for an interview: identify the render trigger and its scope first (colocate state), then reach for memoization only for props that must cross a boundary you can't otherwise avoid re-rendering.
tradeoffs: Reaching for `useMemo`/`useCallback` everywhere "defensively" has real costs — extra memory for cached values/closures and a dependency array that's one more thing to get wrong (a missing dependency silently freezes a callback with stale values) — so the right habit is to memoize only props passed into a `React.memo`'d child, not every function in a component. State colocation is usually the higher-leverage fix in real profiling sessions like this one, because it removes the re-render at the source rather than papering over it further down the tree; reach for it before reaching for `memo`. An alternative to colocation here would be lifting `message` into a dedicated context or state management library so multiple deeply nested components could read it without prop drilling, but that's solving a different problem (prop drilling) and would be over-engineering for a two-sibling case like this.
followUps: How would React DevTools Profiler's flame graph have looked before and after this fix, concretely?
When would state colocation not be possible (both siblings genuinely need the same fast-changing state) — what would you do then?
Why doesn't React.memo alone fix this even before the colocation change — walk through exactly why config and onKick fail the shallow comparison?
What's the risk of over-applying useCallback to every event handler in a large component tree?

title: Fix incorrect useEffect usage
scenario: A junior engineer on the ERP team added a "sync cart total to the order summary" feature, but QA reports the browser tab freezes after adding two or three line items to a purchase order, and the network tab shows a runaway stream of duplicate save requests. You're asked to find the useEffect misuse causing this and fix it — including recognizing which piece of logic shouldn't be an effect at all.
requirements: Identify the missing/incorrect dependency causing an infinite loop
Determine which logic here is actually an event handler in disguise and should not run in an effect
Fix the infinite loop without introducing a missed-update bug (stale total after a line item changes)
Avoid firing a save request more often than necessary (e.g. one per meaningful change, not per render)
Explain the general rule for "should this be an effect?" you used to decide
bugs:
- The first effect includes `total` in its own dependency array even though it only reads `lineItems` — since the effect itself calls `setTotal`, this creates a direct infinite loop: effect runs -> sets total -> total changed -> effect dependency array includes total -> effect runs again -> ... forever. This is the tab-freezing bug.
- Computing `total` from `lineItems` doesn't need an effect at all — it's a pure derivation of existing state ("can I compute this during render from props/state I already have?" — yes), so it should just be a plain `const total = lineItems.reduce(...)` computed inline (or memoized with `useMemo` if expensive), not stored in its own state + synced via effect. This is the textbook "you don't need an effect for this" case.
- The second effect fires `api.saveOrder` on every render where `orderId`, `lineItems`, or `total` differ — combined with the first bug, this means a save request fires on every single iteration of the infinite loop too, explaining the runaway network requests QA saw.
- Autosaving on every `lineItems` change (i.e., on every keystroke/quantity tick if line items are edited granularly) is likely far more frequent than intended; this is a case where the *save* is a legitimate side effect but probably needs debouncing, distinct from the total calculation which shouldn't be an effect at all.
explanation: `total` is removed as its own piece of state entirely; it's now computed directly from `lineItems` during render via `useMemo`, which both eliminates the possibility of the two ever disagreeing (no "stale total" bug, since it's recalculated from the source of truth every render `lineItems` changes) and removes the infinite-loop-causing effect altogether — there is nothing to set, so there is no re-trigger. This follows the general rule for "should this be an effect?": if a value can be computed synchronously from props/state already available during render, it should be, not stored in its own state and synchronized via an effect — effects are for synchronizing with something *outside* React (the network, a subscription, the DOM, local storage), not for keeping two pieces of React state in sync with each other. The remaining effect (autosave) is a legitimate side effect since it talks to an external system (the API), so it correctly stays in `useEffect`; it's fixed by debouncing with a `setTimeout`/cleanup pair, so rapid successive `lineItems` changes (e.g. quickly editing quantities on several items) collapse into a single save 800ms after the user pauses, rather than firing one request per intermediate state.
tradeoffs: Debouncing the autosave with a fixed 800ms delay is simple but means the user could navigate away just after making a change and lose it unsaved; a production version would also flush the pending save on unmount/navigation (e.g. in the effect's cleanup or a `beforeunload` handler) as a follow-up hardening step. Using `useMemo` for `total` here is a minor optimization rather than a correctness requirement, since `lineItems.reduce` over a purchase order's line items is cheap — the real fix is removing the effect-based derivation, not the memoization; it's worth being clear in an interview that memoizing a derived value and not-using-an-effect-for-it are two separate decisions. An alternative to a raw `setTimeout` debounce is a proper debounce utility or a mutation library (TanStack Query's `useMutation` plus a debounced trigger) which also gives you loading/error state for the save itself, worth mentioning as the more complete version of this fix.
followUps: What's the general heuristic for "does this state need an effect, or can it be computed during render" — walk through a few more examples?
Why does including total in the first effect's dependency array specifically cause an infinite loop, step by step?
How would you handle flushing a pending debounced save if the user navigates away before it fires?
When is it actually correct to sync one piece of state to another via an effect, if ever?

title: Fix a Next.js hydration mismatch
scenario: The tax workflow dashboard shows "Filing due in 3 days" style relative countdowns on each filing card. After a recent deploy, the browser console fills with hydration mismatch warnings, and QA notices the countdown text visibly flickers/changes right after page load — sometimes showing a completely different day count for a split second before "fixing itself."
requirements: Identify why the server-rendered HTML and the client's first render disagree
Fix the mismatch without disabling SSR for the whole page (no blanket "use client" escape hatch that defeats the point of SSR)
Ensure the relative time text is stable on first paint and updates correctly afterward (e.g. every minute)
Explain why Date.now()/Math.random()/window access during render is unsafe in a component that's server-rendered
Keep the fix general enough to reuse across other components that show relative/local time
bugs:
- `Date.now()` is called directly during render, which runs both on the server (at request/build time) and again on the client during hydration — these two calls happen at genuinely different wall-clock moments (even if only milliseconds or seconds apart), so `daysRemaining` can differ between server-rendered HTML and the client's first render, exactly what a hydration mismatch is: React expects the client's first render to produce identical output to the server-rendered markup it's attaching event listeners to, and warns loudly (and can discard/re-render the subtree) when it doesn't.
- Because the component is presumably a Server Component (or a Client Component whose first render still must match SSR output) with no special handling, "the day boundary rolled over between SSR and hydration" is a real, not just theoretical, occasion for this bug — e.g. if the page is rendered by a CDN/cache slightly before the user's browser loads it.
- The countdown never updates after mount — even once hydration succeeds, "due in 3 days" will silently become wrong at midnight without a page refresh, since nothing re-triggers a re-render on the client to recompute it.
- Reaching for a blanket `'use client'` and computing everything client-only would silence the warning but throws away the benefit of server-rendering the rest of the card (client name, static content) and still leaves a flash of "wrong then corrected" text on load unless handled carefully.
explanation: The root cause is that `Date.now()` (like `Math.random()` or reading `window`) is non-deterministic across two separate render passes — the server's render and the client's hydration render — and Next.js/React requires those two passes to produce identical markup, because React reuses the server HTML and only attaches event listeners/state during hydration rather than re-rendering from scratch; any difference is a hydration mismatch. The fix isolates the time-dependent part into its own small client component and gives it a two-phase render: the first client render (which must match the server) renders a static, non-time-dependent placeholder ("Calculating…") exactly as the server would have, and only *after* mount does a `useEffect` read the real clock and update state — since effects only run on the client post-hydration, this is a safe place to introduce non-determinism, and any resulting re-render is a normal client-side update, not a hydration diff. A `setInterval` inside the same effect keeps the countdown accurate as time passes (recomputing every minute) and is cleaned up on unmount. Keeping only `RelativeDueDate` as a client component — rather than making the whole `FilingCard` client-side — preserves server rendering (and its performance/SEO/streaming benefits) for the static parts of the card, which is the general pattern for fixing hydration issues without a blanket `'use client'` escape hatch.
tradeoffs: Rendering a placeholder ("Calculating…") for a brief instant is a minor, deliberate trade-off — a tiny flash of neutral text instead of a wrong-then-corrected number — which is much less jarring than the flicker QA originally reported, and can be softened further with a skeleton/pulse style. An alternative is to compute the initial value on the server (pass a server-computed `daysRemaining` as a prop) and only use the client effect to keep it updating afterward — this avoids the placeholder entirely for the very first paint, at the cost of the server and client needing to agree the value is "close enough" (still technically non-deterministic, but usually acceptable if the two computations happen within the same request/response cycle). For less precision-critical relative-time UI, a library like `date-fns`'s `formatDistanceToNow` combined with the same "compute after mount" pattern avoids re-deriving the day-math by hand.
followUps: Why does React specifically warn about hydration mismatches instead of silently using the client's version — what would silently swallowing it risk?
How would you apply this same pattern to a component that needs to read window.innerWidth or localStorage during render?
What's the trade-off between the "placeholder then client-compute" approach here versus passing a server-computed initial value as a prop?
How would you catch hydration mismatches like this one in CI before they reach production?

title: Separate Server and Client Components correctly (Next.js App Router)
scenario: A new engineer building the audit dashboard's client detail page marked the whole page `'use client'` "to be safe" after hitting a server/client error, and in doing so accidentally shipped the internal audit-scoring API key to the browser bundle — caught by a routine bundle-analysis check before release, but flagged as a near-miss security incident. You're asked to restructure the page with correct Server/Client boundaries.
requirements: Identify exactly which part of the page actually needs to be a Client Component (interactivity, hooks, browser APIs) versus what does not
Move any secret/API-key usage into a Server Component or Route Handler, never into client-bundled code
Keep data fetching on the server where possible instead of fetching client-side after mount
Pass only the minimum necessary serializable data down from Server to Client Components as props
Explain the rule of thumb for deciding the client/server boundary, so the team doesn't repeat this mistake
bugs:
- `AUDIT_SCORING_API_KEY` is read from `process.env` in a `'use client'` file — even though it looks like a server-only env var, marking the file client-side means Next.js bundles this module (and the literal key value, once inlined at build time if it were ever accidentally exposed via NEXT_PUBLIC_ or otherwise reachable) for the browser; more critically, the `fetch` call using it as a Bearer token runs in the browser, sending the key in a network request any user can inspect via devtools — this is the near-miss security incident.
- The entire page is `'use client'`, but the only things that actually need client-side interactivity are the notes textarea and its save button; the client name, initial data fetch, and (especially) the scoring call have zero reason to run in the browser.
- Both data fetches happen in a `useEffect` after mount, meaning the page ships an empty shell, then waterfalls two client-side network requests — slower than fetching on the server during the initial render, and it also means the risk score fetch (which needs the secret key) has no business being client-triggered at all.
- `params.clientId` is used directly as a dependency array item, which works but is a smaller symptom of the same "does this need to be client-side" issue — none of this needs `useEffect` if the data is fetched server-side instead.
explanation: The page component drops `'use client'` entirely and becomes an `async` Server Component, which lets it `await` both `getClient` and `getRiskScore` directly during server rendering — this fixes the secret-key leak because `getRiskScore`'s code, including the `Authorization: Bearer` header built from `process.env.AUDIT_SCORING_API_KEY`, now only ever executes on the server; it's never included in the client JavaScript bundle and the key value never appears in any request the browser makes. The rule of thumb applied here: a piece of UI needs `'use client'` only if it needs interactivity (event handlers), component state/effects, or browser-only APIs — everything else should default to a Server Component, since that's the App Router's default and gives you server-side data fetching, zero client JS for that piece, and safe secret access for free. Only `NotesEditor` — the textarea and save button, which genuinely need `useState` and `onClick` — is extracted into its own file marked `'use client'`, and it receives just `clientId` (a plain string, safely serializable across the server/client boundary) as a prop, not the whole `client` object or anything containing sensitive data it doesn't need. Fetching `client` and `riskScore` in parallel with `Promise.all` during the server render also removes the client-side fetch waterfall the original code had, improving perceived load time.
tradeoffs: Making the whole page a Server Component means the page can no longer show a fine-grained client-side loading spinner while individual fetches resolve; Next.js's `loading.tsx` (route-level Suspense boundary) or wrapping slower data in `<Suspense>` with a client-rendered fallback is the idiomatic replacement, worth mentioning as a follow-up refinement. Passing only `clientId` (not the full `client` object) to `NotesEditor` is deliberately minimal — it means if `NotesEditor` ever needs another field from `client`, it must be added explicitly as a prop, which is slightly more code than passing the whole object, but keeps the client bundle boundary auditable at a glance (you can see exactly what data crosses into client code). If `getRiskScore` were slow, doing it in `Promise.all` with `getClient` means the whole page waits for the slower of the two; splitting the risk score into its own `<Suspense>`-wrapped async Server Component would let the client name render first — a reasonable next iteration once the security issue itself is fixed.
followUps: How would you add a loading skeleton for just the risk score while the client name renders immediately, using Suspense?
What's the actual mechanism by which "use client" causes a module's code (and referenced env vars) to end up in the browser bundle?
How would you catch a secret-in-client-bundle mistake like this automatically in CI, rather than relying on a manual bundle-analysis check?
When, if ever, would fetching data in a useEffect inside a Client Component still be the right call in an App Router app?

title: Design Next.js route structure for a multi-role app
scenario: The coaching marketplace is expanding from a single mixed dashboard into three distinct experiences — coach, learner, and admin — each with different navigation, layouts, and permitted routes, but sharing some components (session detail, messaging) and a common design system. You're asked to lay out the App Router route structure before the team starts building each role's screens in parallel.
requirements: Give each role its own route namespace with role-appropriate layouts and navigation
Share common layout chrome (header, design tokens) without duplicating it three times
Guard each role's routes so a learner can't navigate into /admin/* pages even by typing the URL
Allow a shared route (like a session detail page) to render differently depending on which role is viewing it, without three copies of the page
Keep the routing structure statically clear from the folder layout alone (any engineer can find "where does the admin refunds page live" quickly)
bugs:
- All three roles share one flat `/dashboard` namespace with in-component `if (user.role === ...)` branching, so there's no structural (folder-level) way to see which routes belong to which role, and no single layout enforcement point per role — every page has to remember to check permissions itself.
- Nothing prevents a learner from directly navigating to an admin-only URL; any guarding that exists is buried inside individual page components rather than enforced at the route/layout level, making it easy for a new admin-only page to be added without anyone remembering to add the check.
- Shared pages like session detail have no clean mechanism for "render differently per role" other than branchy conditionals scattered through one component, which grows unmaintainable as more roles/permissions are added.
- No shared layout structure — common chrome (header, design tokens) presumably gets copy-pasted or awkwardly conditionally rendered inside each role's dashboard view rather than living in one shared layout.
explanation: Route groups (`(app)`) let the header/design-tokens layout wrap all three roles' subtrees without adding a URL segment, while each role gets its own folder (`coach/`, `learner/`, `admin/`) with its own `layout.tsx` for role-specific navigation — this makes "where does the admin refunds page live" answerable by reading the folder tree (`app/(app)/admin/refunds/[id]/page.tsx`) rather than hunting through conditional JSX. Guarding moves from scattered in-component checks to `middleware.ts`, matched against path prefixes (`/admin/:path*`, etc.) — this is enforced once, for every route under each prefix, so a new admin page automatically inherits the guard just by living under `app/(app)/admin/`, and a learner typing an admin URL directly is redirected before any admin page code runs. The shared `sessions/[id]` route stays a single URL and single data-fetching page, but delegates role-specific rendering to small, separately named view components (`AdminSessionView`, `CoachSessionView`, `LearnerSessionView`) via a clean switch, rather than one large component full of `if (role === ...)` branches — each view can grow independently without the others' JSX cluttering it. As with the earlier labs, middleware here is a routing/UX guard only: the underlying data fetch (`getSessionData`) and any mutations (kicking a participant, refunding a session) must still independently verify the caller's role and resource ownership server-side, since middleware doesn't protect direct API calls.
tradeoffs: Per-role layouts mean some duplicated navigation-shell boilerplate across `coach/layout.tsx`, `learner/layout.tsx`, and `admin/layout.tsx`; a shared `<RoleNav role={...} items={...} />` component factors out the common structure while still letting each layout pass its own nav items, which is usually worth doing once the three navs stabilize. Middleware-based path-prefix guarding is simple and centralized but coarse — it can't express "a coach can view this specific session only if they're the assigned coach," which still needs a resource-level check inside `getSessionData`/the page itself (or the API layer) as described in lab 3's trade-offs. An alternative to one shared `sessions/[id]` route with a role switch is genuinely separate routes per role (`/coach/sessions/[id]`, `/learner/sessions/[id]`) if the roles' views diverge enough in URL semantics (e.g. different tabs/sub-routes per role) — the shared-route approach shown here is right when the underlying resource and top-level page are conceptually the same thing viewed differently, not fundamentally different flows.
followUps: How would you avoid duplicating the nav-shell boilerplate across the three role layouts?
Where exactly would you add a resource-level check ("this coach can only see their own sessions") on top of the role-level middleware guard?
What would you do differently if a user could hold two roles at once (e.g. someone who is both a coach and an admin)?
How would you structure this if the admin section itself needed sub-roles (e.g. support-agent vs super-admin)?

title: Build payment status handling UI (Stripe/Razorpay redirect + webhook)
scenario: Coaches on the marketplace pay a subscription fee via Razorpay to keep their profile listed; learners pay per-session via Stripe. After checkout, both are redirected back to the app while the actual payment confirmation arrives asynchronously via webhook to your backend — so the page the user lands on right after paying often doesn't yet know the final outcome. Support has tickets from users confused by a page that says "processing" forever after a successful payment.
requirements: Handle all real payment states distinctly: pending, succeeded, failed, and requires-retry
Poll or subscribe for the authoritative status rather than trusting only the redirect URL's query params
Give the user a clear retry action on failure, and avoid double-charging on retry
Never trust or act on a client-supplied "success" query param as proof of payment — the webhook-confirmed backend state is the source of truth
Handle the case where the webhook hasn't arrived yet by the time the user lands on the return page (show pending, keep checking)
bugs:
- This trusts a client-supplied `searchParams.status` query param as the actual payment outcome — that value comes back on the redirect URL from the payment provider's client-side flow and is trivially editable by the user (anyone can append `?status=success` to the URL) or can be wrong/stale if the redirect fires before the webhook-confirmed charge actually settles; it must never be treated as proof of payment.
- There's no polling or subscription to the authoritative backend state at all — the page renders once based on the URL and never checks again, so a payment that was still "pending" at redirect time (webhook not yet processed) is stuck showing "Processing your payment..." forever, exactly the support tickets described.
- No retry action wired up for the failed case — just static text with no button/link back to checkout, and no safeguard mentioned against double-charging if a user does retry (e.g. re-using the same payment intent/order id vs. creating a new charge).
- No distinction between "genuinely failed" and "still pending, webhook not arrived yet" — both would currently show up under whatever the query param happens to say, conflating two very different states requiring different UI.
explanation: The return page now reads only `orderId` from the URL — a stable identifier, not a claimed outcome — and hands off to `PaymentStatusPoller`, which polls `/api/orders/:id/status`, a backend endpoint whose value is written exclusively by the signature-verified webhook handler (`updateOrderStatusFromWebhook`), never by anything the client says. This is what makes the backend state authoritative: a user editing the return URL's query params has no way to change what `/api/orders/:id/status` reports, because that value only changes when Razorpay/Stripe's own signed webhook call updates it. Polling every 3 seconds (capped at `maxAttempts`) directly fixes the "stuck on processing forever" bug: if the webhook hasn't landed yet when the user arrives, the UI honestly shows "Confirming your payment…" and keeps checking rather than guessing from the redirect, and naturally resolves to `succeeded`/`failed` once the webhook does land. The retry flow calls a backend endpoint that resumes the *same* `orderId`/payment intent rather than starting a brand-new checkout, which is the mechanism that prevents a double charge — the payment provider's API is told "continue this order," not "charge again from scratch." Webhook signature verification (`verifyWebhookSignature`) is essential and shown explicitly because an unverified webhook endpoint would let anyone POST a fake "payment succeeded" event directly to your server, which is an even more direct attack than trusting a query param.
tradeoffs: Polling is simple to reason about but adds a request every few seconds during the confirmation window; a WebSocket or Server-Sent Events push from the backend (notified the instant the webhook lands) would resolve status faster and with less network chatter, at the cost of needing that real-time infrastructure — a reasonable trade to bring up as "if this needed to feel instantaneous." Capping polling attempts and falling back to a "still processing, we'll email you" message avoids leaving the user staring at a spinner indefinitely if something is genuinely stuck upstream (e.g. the webhook delivery itself failed) — worth adding a manual "check again" button and a support contact once the cap is hit. Reusing the same order id for retries is the correct approach for avoiding double charges, but it requires the backend's order/payment-intent model to explicitly support "retry this failed attempt" as a state transition, which is a backend design decision this frontend lab assumes exists — worth flagging as a dependency in a real project plan.
followUps: Why is verifying the webhook signature non-negotiable, and what could an attacker do if that check were skipped?
How would you replace the 3-second polling with a WebSocket push once the webhook lands, and what would change in this component?
What UI would you show if polling hits its max attempts without resolving to succeeded or failed?
How does the backend guarantee a retry resumes the same order instead of creating a duplicate charge — what would you ask a backend engineer to confirm here?

title: Build a timezone-safe session/booking time display
scenario: The coaching marketplace books sessions across many timezones — a coach in Berlin, a learner in Bengaluru. A recent bug report: a session stored as "3:00 PM" showed correctly for the coach who booked it but appeared as the wrong hour for the learner, and a separate ticket describes a session that "disappeared" from someone's calendar around a Daylight Saving Time transition weekend.
requirements: Store and transmit all session times in UTC, never in a fixed "local" string
Render times in each viewer's own local timezone, derived from their browser/profile setting
Handle DST transitions correctly (a session time doesn't shift or disappear across a DST boundary)
Avoid the Next.js hydration mismatch trap from lab 14 when rendering a timezone-dependent value on a server-rendered page
Show the timezone explicitly in the UI when it might not be obvious to the viewer (e.g. "3:00 PM IST")
bugs:
- The fundamental bug is upstream of this component: `clientLocalTime` is a naive datetime string with no timezone information baked in at all, so it's ambiguous the moment it's read by anyone other than the exact person/timezone that produced it — this is why the learner in Bengaluru saw the wrong hour: the string was never converted, just displayed as-is regardless of who's viewing it.
- Because there's no UTC offset stored, there's no way to correctly compute what that moment in time is for a different timezone, and no way to disambiguate a time that falls in a DST "fall back" repeated hour or is skipped entirely in a "spring forward" gap.
- If this were fixed to compute a timezone-aware render, doing it directly during a server-rendered component's render (assuming this page is SSR'd) would reintroduce the lab 14 hydration mismatch, since the server doesn't know the viewer's timezone and the client does.
- No timezone abbreviation/offset shown in the UI, so even a correctly-converted time is ambiguous to a user unsure whether it's already been adjusted to their local time or not.
explanation: The real fix starts at the data layer: sessions are stored and transmitted as `startsAtUtc`, a UTC ISO 8601 string, which is an unambiguous, absolute point in time regardless of who reads it — this is what makes correct per-viewer rendering possible at all, since a naive "local time string" with no offset can never be reliably converted for a different viewer.
