Rendering uses `Intl.DateTimeFormat` with an explicit `timeZone` option set to the *viewer's* IANA timezone (`Intl.DateTimeFormat().resolvedOptions().timeZone`, e.g. `"Asia/Kolkata"`), which correctly and automatically accounts for DST rules for that specific zone and date — this is the mechanism that fixes both the "wrong hour for a different viewer" bug and the DST-transition bug, since `Intl`'s timezone database (not manual offset math) knows exactly when each zone's DST boundaries fall. `timeZoneName: 'short'` appends the zone abbreviation (e.g. "IST", "CET") directly in the formatted output, satisfying the explicit-timezone requirement without extra string concatenation. To avoid the lab 14 hydration mismatch, the component renders a neutral placeholder on the server and first client pass, then computes the real, viewer-timezone-dependent string inside a `useEffect` (which only runs post-hydration on the client) — the server genuinely cannot know the viewer's timezone reliably (it isn't sent with a normal page request), so deferring the computation to the client, after mount, is the correct application of the same pattern from lab 14, not a workaround. On the write side, converting a coach's locally-picked time into UTC before sending it to the API must use their specific IANA timezone (not a raw numeric offset, which is exactly what breaks across DST) via a timezone-aware library.
tradeoffs: Using `Intl.DateTimeFormat` (built into the browser) avoids adding a dependency for basic formatting, but timezone *conversion* on the write path (turning a picked local time into UTC) is fiddly and error-prone to hand-roll correctly across DST edge cases — a library like `date-fns-tz` or Luxon is worth the dependency for that specific operation, even if display formatting stays native. Deferring the real formatted time to a post-mount effect means a brief placeholder flash on every page load, similar to lab 14's trade-off; if server-side viewer timezone were available (e.g. stored in the user's profile and passed to the server render instead of relying on the browser's `Intl` timezone), the initial server render could show the correct time immediately, removing the placeholder step entirely — worth mentioning as a stronger fix if a user profile timezone field already exists. Storing a fixed "timezone" string per user profile (rather than always trusting the browser's current `Intl` timezone) matters for cases like an email notification generated server-side, where there's no "current browser" to ask — that's a case where you do want a persisted profile-level timezone rather than only ever deriving it live.
followUps: Why does converting local-picked time to UTC need the specific IANA timezone rather than just "UTC+5:30" as a fixed offset?
How would you render this correctly for a server-generated email (no browser Intl available) versus a live web page?
What would you test specifically to catch a regression at a DST transition boundary?
If a user's profile has a stored preferred timezone that differs from their current browser timezone (e.g. traveling), which should win, and why?

title: Preserve filter/sort/page state in the URL
scenario: On the ERP inventory table, users apply filters (warehouse, category), sort by a column, and page through results — then hit the back button after opening an item detail page, only to land back on an unfiltered, unsorted, page-1 view, losing all their context. Product wants the URL to fully capture this state so back/forward and refresh all behave correctly, and a filtered view can be bookmarked or shared with a coworker.
requirements: Reflect filter, sort, and page state in the URL search params, not only in component state
Support the browser back/forward buttons correctly (returning to a previous filter state, not just a previous page number)
Make the initial state on page load derive from the URL (so a shared/bookmarked link reproduces the exact view)
Avoid pushing a new history entry on every keystroke of a search filter (debounce, or replace instead of push for minor changes)
Keep the component's internal logic reading a single source of truth rather than syncing URL and local state in two directions ad hoc
bugs:
- All state (`warehouse`, `sortBy`, `page`) lives only in local component `useState`, entirely disconnected from the URL — navigating away and back (or refreshing) always resets to the defaults, which is exactly the reported bug, and the view can never be bookmarked or shared meaningfully since the URL never changes.
- The browser's back button has nothing to go "back" to for filter changes, since changing a filter never creates a navigation/history entry at all — from the browser's perspective, filtering doesn't count as navigation.
- If this were naively fixed by calling `router.push` on every state change, an initial-state derivation is still missing (nothing reads the URL on mount to initialize `warehouse`/`sortBy`/`page`), so even with the URL updating, a fresh load of a "shared" URL would show default state while the URL itself has the filters in it — a subtler version of the same bug.
- No distinction between "structural" navigation (changing the page number, changing warehouse) which should push a new history entry, and something like live-typing a search box, which should debounce and use replace to avoid spamming history with one entry per keystroke.
explanation: `useTableUrlState` reads `warehouse`, `sortBy`, and `page` directly from `useSearchParams()` on every render rather than mirroring them into local `useState`, which makes the URL the single source of truth — there's no two-way sync to get out of sync, because there's only ever one place the state lives. Initial load (including a bookmarked/shared link) works correctly for free, since the very first render already derives its values from whatever the URL contains, with sensible defaults (`'all'`, `'name'`, `1`) only when a param is absent. `router.push` is used for filter/sort/page changes, which creates a new browser history entry for each — this is what makes the back button work as expected: navigating back moves to the previous URL, whose search params represent the previous filter/sort/page state, and the component naturally re-renders with those restored values with no extra code. Changing the warehouse or sort also resets `page` to 1 in the same `setParams` call, mirroring the correct behavior from lab 8's pagination-reset requirement, but now expressed as a URL change instead of local state. `router.replace` is available (and would be used for a debounced live-search-box input) specifically to avoid creating one history entry per keystroke, which would otherwise make the back button nearly useless by forcing the user to click back many times to undo one search.
tradeoffs: Encoding all filter/sort/page state in the URL is the right call for a table like this, meant to be referenced, bookmarked, and navigated with the back button, but it does mean the URL can get long/ugly with many filters, and very large or non-primitive filter state (e.g. a multi-select with dozens of ids) may be better serialized compactly (comma-joined ids, or a short encoded token) rather than one param per field. Using `router.push` per filter change is correct for the "these are meaningfully different views" case, but for something like a live free-text search box, debouncing the URL update itself (not just the fetch) and using `replace` instead of `push` avoids flooding browser history — this hook's `replace` option exists for exactly that case, worth calling out explicitly if a search field were added. Deriving state from `useSearchParams()` on every render is simple and correct but means every param read triggers a new URLSearchParams parse; for a table with many params this is negligible, but worth knowing it's not "free" the way plain local state is.
followUps: How would you add a debounced search text field to this table without spamming browser history on every keystroke?
What changes if you need to support multi-select filters (e.g. several warehouses at once) in the URL?
How would you keep the URL and fetched data in sync if two tabs are open on the same URL and one changes a filter?
Why is deriving state from the URL on every render safer here than syncing local state to the URL with a useEffect?

title: Build an accessible reusable modal component (useModal hook + portal)
scenario: Several teams across the agriculture marketplace (event booking confirmation, a delete-listing confirmation, an image lightbox) have each built their own slightly-different modal, and an accessibility audit flagged that none of them trap focus correctly or restore focus to the triggering element on close — a screen reader user reported getting "lost" after closing a dialog. You're asked to build one shared `useModal` hook plus a portal-rendered `Modal` component the whole app can standardize on.
requirements: Trap Tab/Shift+Tab focus within the open modal (focus never escapes to background content)
Close on Escape key, and on backdrop click, without closing on a click that started inside the modal and was dragged out
Restore focus to the element that opened the modal when it closes
Render via a portal to a dedicated DOM node, not inline in the component tree (to escape parent overflow/z-index issues)
Be SSR-safe for Next.js: no access to window/document at module scope, and the portal target must only be created/queried in the browser
bugs:
- No focus trapping at all: Tab/Shift+Tab move focus into background page content behind the modal, which is both disorienting for sighted keyboard users and a real accessibility violation for screen reader users (the reported bug).
- No Escape-key handling, and no focus restoration — after closing, focus is simply wherever it happened to be (often the document body), so a screen reader user loses their place entirely instead of landing back on the "Delete" button that opened the dialog.
- Rendered inline in the component tree (not via a portal), so it's vulnerable to being clipped or stacked incorrectly by any ancestor with `overflow: hidden` or a conflicting `z-index` — a common bug across the app's several hand-rolled modals.
- `onClick={onClose}` on the backdrop closes even if the mousedown started inside `.modal-content` and the drag/mouseup ended on the backdrop (e.g. selecting text and releasing outside) — this is the "closes on a click that shouldn't count" bug, since a single onClick can't distinguish where the interaction started.
- Nothing here is SSR-safe yet, though this simple version doesn't happen to touch `document`/`window` at module scope — the portal version needs explicit care not to introduce that when created.
explanation: `useModal` centralizes all the accessibility-critical mechanics so no team has to reimplement them: `open()` captures `document.activeElement` (whatever had focus right before opening — the trigger button) into `triggerRef`, and `close()` calls `.focus()` on it again, which is what restores the screen reader/keyboard user's position after the dialog closes, directly fixing the "getting lost" report. The focus trap works by querying all focusable descendants of the modal content on open (via `FOCUSABLE_SELECTOR`) and listening for `Tab`/`Shift+Tab` at the document level; when focus is on the last focusable element and the user tabs forward (or on the first and shifts back), `preventDefault` stops the browser's default focus movement and manually wraps it to the other end — this is what keeps Tab cycling within the modal instead of escaping to background content. The backdrop close logic separates `onMouseDown` (recording whether the press started directly on the backdrop, not inside `.modal-content`) from `onMouseUp` (only closing if both the down and up events targeted the backdrop itself), which correctly ignores a text-selection drag that starts inside the modal and releases outside it. `createPortal` renders the modal into a dedicated `#modal-root` node appended to `document.body`, escaping any ancestor's `overflow`/`z-index` constraints; critically, the DOM node is created and queried only inside a `useEffect` (which never runs during SSR), and the component returns `null` until `portalTarget` state is set, so no `document` access ever happens at module scope or during the server render — this is what makes it SSR-safe for Next.js.
tradeoffs: Hand-rolling the focus-trap query selector list is a maintenance surface (it needs to stay in sync with whatever focusable elements teams put inside modals, e.g. custom components with a nonstandard tabindex pattern); a library like `focus-trap-react` or Radix UI's Dialog primitive solves this more robustly and handles edge cases (dynamically added/removed focusable children, nested modals) that this lab's version doesn't attempt. Restoring focus via a captured `document.activeElement` ref is simple and correct for the common case, but breaks if the triggering element is removed from the DOM while the modal is open (e.g. the row that opened a modal gets deleted by another action) — a production version needs a fallback focus target for that case. Creating the portal target lazily in an effect (rather than assuming a static `#modal-root` div exists in the page's root HTML) is slightly more code but avoids a hard dependency on app-shell markup, making the `Modal`/`useModal` pair a truly drop-in, portable pair usable from any page without additional setup.
followUps: How would you handle a modal that needs to open another modal on top of it (nested modals) with this focus-trap implementation?
What happens to focus restoration if the triggering element is removed from the DOM while the modal is open, and how would you handle that?
Why must the portal target be created inside a useEffect rather than during render, specifically in a Next.js SSR context?
How would you test the focus-trap Tab/Shift+Tab wrapping behavior in an automated test?
What ARIA attributes beyond role="dialog" and aria-modal="true" would you consider adding, and why (e.g. aria-labelledby)?
